title: Acting service and the Federal Vacancies Reform Act
shortTitle: Acting service and the Federal Vacancies Reform Act
summary: Temporary acting service can maintain administration during vacancies, subject to statutory eligibility, duration, agency-specific succession rules, and constitutional officer requirements.
notes:
The Federal Vacancies Reform Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 3345–3349d, supplies a general route for temporarily performing the duties of many vacant offices normally filled by presidential appointment with Senate consent. The reading distinguishes this statutory route from constitutional recess appointments and from succession provisions in an agency’s own statute. The ordinary 210-day period has qualifications, including periods while certain nominations are pending; the excerpt also describes statutory provisions that independently designate an acting officer. Members of multi-member independent boards fall within a specified exclusion, so the FVRA did not solve the NLRB quorum problem.

The examples show why each vacancy requires attention to the governing text. The CFPB controversy involved competing claims under the Dodd-Frank succession provision and the President’s FVRA choice of OMB Director Mick Mulvaney. Leandra English failed to obtain a preliminary injunction and later dropped the suit; that procedural result should not be recast as a Supreme Court settlement. Matthew Whitaker’s appointment raised a separate question whether temporary service at the head of a department makes an official a principal officer. OLC and several lower courts relied on the temporary nature of service in treating him as inferior. The DHS example concerns a later statute that removed the FVRA as a presidential source for determining succession and vested that task in the Secretary. The Julie Su example involves the Labor Department’s own succession statute and the consequences of a pending nomination. These are the textbook’s historical examples, not a statement of personnel or legal conditions in 2026.

Delegating functions can also preserve operations without filling the office. The FVRA’s definition of a function or duty focuses on tasks legally assigned exclusively to the specified officer. The editors and Anne Joseph O’Connell explain that delegable work may therefore move to lower officials after acting-service limits expire. This distinction creates both administrative continuity and opportunities to weaken the practical force of Senate confirmation. A delegation’s validity still depends on the law authorizing it; a title such as “performing the duties” does not itself establish authority.
